Vendored three.js r0.184.0 and Google Fonts — provenance record
===============================================================

Why these files are here at all
-------------------------------

This page makes no external request. Before vendoring it fetched three.js
from cdn.jsdelivr.net and two font families from fonts.googleapis.com /
fonts.gstatic.com, which handed the visitor's IP to two third parties on
every load. The people who open a memorial to Ukraine's fallen should not
have their visit logged by anyone, and fonts.googleapis.com is not reliably
reachable from every region this page is meant to be read in.

This follows the same pattern as PulseMask's vendor/ directory — flat
vendored files, a fonts.css of rewritten @font-face rules, per-family OFL
text, and this record. It diverges in one place, documented below: the
three.js builds here are minified.

three.js
--------

The import map maps three, three/webgpu and three/tsl at ./vendor/. Note
that three.tsl.min.js imports the BARE specifier 'three/webgpu' and
three.webgpu.min.js imports './three.core.min.js' relatively — so all three
files must stay side by side and the import map must keep the three/webgpu
entry.

MINIFIED, unlike PulseMask's vendor/ which ships the readable builds. That
is a deliberate divergence, not drift. The readable trio is 3.5 MB against
1.0 MB minified, and this page is opened by families on connections inside
Ukraine; 2.5 MB is real seconds there. Nobody steps through three.js
internals on a deployed memorial, and the re-verification recipe below works
the same either way. The MIT notice survives minification intact at the top
of all three files, which is what redistribution actually requires.

To confirm a vendored file still matches the authentic upstream release:

    curl -sL https://unpkg.com/three@0.184.0/build/three.webgpu.min.js \
      | openssl dgst -sha384 -binary | openssl base64 -A

sha384, base64 — each verified byte-identical against unpkg on 2026-09-06:

  three.webgpu.min.js  yxymeQ3BZZOUzVptnSOa6Vv/uRqq4cZ3+84ThIL7QpA1xwz0LHhZOS7vdKk6l6ta
    upstream: build/three.webgpu.min.js            (637561 bytes)
  three.core.min.js    /2vXInuUL2LKgd3n86c5RIzG+YC7vk3zYPTknaEkF2H2sauHtaOrS8swZ+MURxU6
    upstream: build/three.core.min.js              (384222 bytes)
    (relative import of three.webgpu.min.js)
  three.tsl.min.js     7MYTCVp8lJhaboioR5rqE3JgHte9xBWv2P807sIlrOKRT1mXXy67vIOVtWT3djU5
    upstream: build/three.tsl.min.js               (23265 bytes)
  OrbitControls.js     4rziNxOBZKQ69i+w+f89KJ55TCYquwchVbByQwmaOeIOXdOU2PLDn3kOfXHwIJC9
    upstream: examples/jsm/controls/OrbitControls.js   (40504 bytes)
    Not minified upstream — three ships examples/jsm as source only. Imports
    the bare specifier 'three', so it resolves through the same import map.

Line endings: .gitattributes marks vendor/** as `-text`, so git performs no
CRLF conversion in either direction. Without that, a clone on Windows would
rewrite the text files here and every hash above would stop matching — the
record would be quietly wrong through no fault of the files.

For reference, the readable builds this replaced — should you ever want to
swap back for debugging, these are PulseMask's own verified hashes and the
files are still in helixPulse/vendor/:

  three.webgpu.js   vatRh9vQy/B/ECoJSF7P/Jg9rF6KVuG/ovU+3Wp/BUaCcpR0DM+a4zCEbQ8Y/RFK
  three.core.js     dw2ooPewaEIrAgl6oFDBmmBWCE9oW9LxRGcfwZ0hLvEprzo202wXl7vCYHRlSnOT
  three.tsl.js      dqftyqccaI6qYFdGtJtugSSe4YKncDgGHttpZJr+lR/vSq18VR5ubqlzEHdGLdJ1

Swapping back means renaming three files AND the three entries in the import
map in Memorial Gallery.dc.html. Then run `node verify.mjs`.

There is no `integrity` block in the import map, and that is not a
downgrade: subresource integrity guards against a THIRD PARTY serving you
different bytes. These files are same-origin now. There is no third party
left to guard against, and anyone who can alter these files can equally
alter the hashes next to them. This record replaces it.

three.js is MIT licensed, (c) 2010-2026 three.js authors. Redistributing it
— which vendoring is — requires the copyright and permission notice to
travel with it; the notice is at the top of all three .min.js files,
intact and unmodified. Minifiers preserve @license blocks precisely so this
stays true.

One line in the READABLE build looks alarming and is not. three.webgpu.js
contains

    import 'https://greggman.github.io/.../webgpu-check-redundant-state-setting.js';

inside a `/*// debugger tools ... //*/` comment block. It is dead code, it
issues no request, and minification strips it entirely — three.webgpu.min.js
contains no reference to that host at all (checked). Do not "fix" it by
editing either file; that would break the byte-for-byte hash match above. If
a future three.js release un-comments it, that is the moment to care.

Fonts
-----

vendor/fonts/ holds Cormorant Garamond (300, 400, 500, 300 italic) and
IBM Plex Mono (400, 500), in the latin, latin-ext, cyrillic and
cyrillic-ext subsets — 24 files, ~492 KB total. Cyrillic is not optional
here: the page is Ukrainian.

Downloaded from the Google Fonts CSS2 API with a modern-Chrome User-Agent
(which is what selects woff2 over the older formats), then rewritten to
relative URLs in fonts.css. Every @font-face keeps its upstream
unicode-range, so a browser still downloads only the subsets a given
visitor actually needs to render the page — vendoring costs no extra
bandwidth over the Google-hosted version.

Both families are SIL Open Font License 1.1. The licence text ships beside
them as fonts/OFL-Cormorant.txt and fonts/OFL-IBMPlex.txt, as the OFL
requires.

To re-fetch a face and confirm it matches upstream, take the URL for the
relevant subset out of:

    curl -sL -A "Mozilla/5.0 ... Chrome/131.0.0.0 ..." \
      "https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Cormorant+Garamond:ital,wght@0,300;0,400;0,500;1,300&display=swap"

Google re-cuts these files on their own schedule (the URLs carry a version
segment, currently v21 for Cormorant Garamond), so a byte difference after
an upstream re-cut is expected and is not evidence of tampering.
